summary: Ignis, developed by Team Eagle, is an interactive dashboard that helps users explore NASA research on fire and combustion in microgravity. It brings selected research materials into a searchable workspace where users can ask questions, review source-linked summaries, explore connections between experiments and materials, and compare or rank findings using visible criteria. Its Cabin Fire-Safety Lab lets users explore how conditions such as material, oxygen level, airflow, pressure, and gravity affect an estimated risk assessment. By connecting research discovery with comparison and scenario exploration, Ignis aims to make complex findings easier to understand in the context of spacecraft and habitat safety. The dashboard is a research aid: its model outputs are exploratory, and users should consult the linked sources and expert guidance before drawing safety conclusions.
details:
Ignis is an interactive research dashboard developed by Team Eagle for the NASA Space Apps Challenge. It helps users explore NASA research on fire and combustion in microgravity by bringing selected papers and structured records into one searchable workspace. Users can ask FlameAI questions, review source-linked summaries, browse experiments and materials, compare findings, explore relationships in a knowledge graph, and rank records using stated criteria.

The app uses a Python FastAPI backend and an HTML, CSS, and JavaScript frontend. Its retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) pipeline searches document passages using a combination of semantic and keyword retrieval, then supplies relevant material to a language model to help generate an answer. A NetworkX knowledge graph connects related research concepts. Ignis also includes a scenario lab where users can vary material, oxygen level, pressure, airflow, and gravity to explore model-estimated risk factors and guidance. These outputs are exploratory and are not certified spacecraft safety assessments.

Ignis addresses the challenge by helping users move from a research question to relevant evidence, comparisons, rankings, and scenario exploration. Its distinctive approach combines conversational search with transparent ranking and interactive research tools, rather than presenting AI as an unqualified authority. We considered the need for traceable sources, clear ranking rules, differences between experimental conditions, and the limits of applying microgravity findings to lunar or Martian habitats. Records marked as proxy or demonstration data are not presented as measured NASA telemetry.
